items.title: Improving, Not Ruining, "Ghostbusters"
items.author: Miss Cellania
items.content: Dustin Ballard of There I Ruined It brings us his Ghostbusters Super Mashup Party for a quick giggle. You have the unmistakable beat from Ray parker Jr's "Ghostbusters" with vocal clips from a variety of other songs. The secret is in the clip selection. Many of them rhyme nicely, which is funny enough, but you also get different clips quoting the movie together, and a tribute to the best Halloween trick-or-treat candy you can receive. Even the way Ballard labeled the clips is designed to bring out the funny.

items.title: Badass Robot
items.author: Miss Cellania
items.content:
Unitree Robotics shows off its new H2-X Kung Fu Legend Guardian robot by first terrifying us, then pulling back to make him seem useful and heroic. This robot can beat your car up while showing off its martial arts moves. It would probably make short work of hauling you in for questioning, and might break your bones while doing it. But oh, it's also useful for protection from bad guys, and its strength and quick reflexes could work for saving lives. But who decides whether it will be used for nefarious or humanitarian purposes? The H2-X Kung Fu Legend Guardian is not yet available, and

might never be sold to the public. The video description has a CYA line: "Please use the robot safely and in a friendly manner." Right. All that said, I'd love to see the outtakes from this production. (via Born in Space)

items.title: The Longest Day of an Election Worker's Life
items.author: Miss Cellania
items.content: The people who work at your local polling place are just people, somewhat more civic minded than most, who volunteer for an increasingly difficult job in order to make our democracy work. They go through training, and do their very best to make the process go smoothly for citizens who cast their votes. Many current and former poll workers came into the comments to say how accurate this video is. The least we can do is appreciate their efforts.

items.title: Bizarre Cephalopod Reproduction
items.author: Miss Cellania
items.content:
Warning: this video contains marine animal sex and plenty of jokes about it. After all, it's a True Facts video from Ze Frank. He offers classroom-friendly version of his videos, but admits that this one might be difficult to translate. 

We've already been through the argument over the plural of octopus many times, but what about cuttlefish? If there are two, is it cuttlefishes or cuttlefish? It's important because it takes two cuttlefish to make babies. But they don't quite cuttle the way you'd expect. For one thing, cephalopod sperm is delivered in biological packages that are about as complex as a space ship to overcome the effects of living underwater. The different species shown here use a variety of methods to deliver them. Male octopi use an arm, which might even detach. Squids, cuttlefish, and octopi know what they're doing, although it looks all wrong to us. The result is eggs laid and a new generation hatched, even if it kills a parent.

items.title: The 2026 Squishing of the Squash
items.author: Miss Cellania
items.content:
Since 1999, when a prize-winning 828 pound pumpkin was donated to the Oregon Zoo, the annual Squishing of the Squash has been a premiere event. Local farmers donate excess produce, and the elephants love it. For them, it's a combination of a ball game, a treasure hunt, and snack time. The crowds of humans love it, too. 

This year, the star of the show was an 18-year-old Asian elephant named Samudra. She was offered a 500 pound pumpkin that was stuffed with apples, sweet potatoes, and lettuce. She had fun playing with the gourd until it cracked open, revealing the surprise banquet. This will be the last Squishing of the Squash in Oregon for Samudra, as she is moving to the St. Louis Zoo next year. Her little sister Tula-Tu, only 20 months old, got her own smaller pumpkin. (via

Laughing Squid)

items.title: Why TV Can't Tell Stories Chronologically
items.author: Miss Cellania
items.content:
The use of the flashback in telling a story has been around forever. In the hands of skilled storyteller, it can be a very effective device. The author wants to control how much the audience knows, and at what point everything can be revealed. However, in modern TV shows, the narrative flashes back and forth so often that the viewer may end up dizzy. These multiple timelines can keep us guessing, or make us just give up. 

Is this just a trend in the art of storytelling? Or is it a way to pad out a too-short main story and make it last through the planned season? Or is it just fun for the cast and crew? The difference between a flashback as a stunt or an effective storytelling device is how necessary it is to making the story coherent and satisfying to watch or read.

items.title: I Have a New Cat!
items.author: Miss Cellania
items.content:
This is Toast. I'm sure it's short for Burnt Toast. He's a 6-year-old Russian Blue, and is twice the size of my other cats. That coloring makes him hard to find and he seems to appear out of nowhere. He's a real sweetie.

Back in the summer, Dr. Dolittle lost her older orange cat Bread to cancer. It was a very difficult time, and she ended up euthanizing him herself.

But what about his companion, Toast? The doctor didn't want to get another cat, and her husband was working in Indiana at the time. She didn't want the cat to be lonely, and besides, they were going to be out of the country for a month this fall. Would I take Toast? Sure! So she brought Toast, and stayed a few days with him. She ended up staying with me four days out of every seven for the next two months, only going home to work. Dr. Engineer joined her here two days a week. Dr. Dolittle really doesn't like living alone. Then her husband got laid off and they are now off in Nepal for a month. 

So Toast lost his cat buddy, his family, and his home. But he gained his heart's desire, the ability to go outside. My cats hated him from the start- after all, he's strange, huge, and hard to see. But Toast is eager to make friends, and after about three months, they are making progress. Marshmallow has decided he's no threat and just ignores him now. Tommy is okay and will let Toast follow him around, and only hisses when he gets too forward. Sundae still growls at him, but is no longer terrified (she stayed outside for a month when he first came). I've even caught a few nose boops between Toast and Tommy and Marshmallow.

Toast has learned how to communicate with me, and goes in and out all day. I think he's testing my limits. Now that it's cold, I make the cats all stay in at night. The other three cats sleep with me at night, but if Sundae is outside, Toast will be on my window table behind the bed when I nap. We are making progress.

items.title: Willowbrook State School
items.author: Miss Cellania
items.content:
It wasn't all that long ago that developmentally disabled children, particularly those with intellectual challenges, were hidden away and cared for in institutions. Out of sight, out of mind. The largest such institution in the US was Willowbrook State School in Staten Island, New York. It had a capacity of 4,000, but by 1965, it housed 6,000 residents. 

By the 1950s, it was clear to the administration that the families of the children living at Willowbrook were not coming to visit, so they could get away with anything. There were unethical medical experiments performed on residents who could neither consent nor complain. After that era, Willowbrook was seriously overcrowded, underfunded, and understaffed. The employees who did their best were forced to take shortcuts because they had too many residents to care for, and other employees were uncaring and abusive. It took a series of exposés to bring attention to the conditions at Willowbrook, and even more horrors were discovered after the school closed.

items.title: Common Words Inspired by Polytheism
items.author: Miss Cellania
items.content:
The influence of the Roman Empire is everywhere. The many gods of the Latin world influence everything because Latin spawned other languages. Latin and Greek mythology gave us the names of the planets and the months. But deities from polytheistic religions came into our language from all over. Our days of the week come from Norse mythology in several languages, and Roman mythology in other languages. Everyday words have religious roots in other languages that we never knew about. Dr. Erica Brozovsky takes us on a tour of how the names of deities ended up in our modern English.

When a stranger comes up with an uncanny smile and tells you to remain calm, you know something weird is up, because that's about the worst thing a stranger can say. But then he says he's from the federal government, and that's even scarier. The twist in this story is that remaining calm is the only thing that will save your life. How can you do that when you're terrified? Or when you're watching a creepy horror story? Well, what normally calms you down when you're stressed? You don't need to answer that; the film will guide you. 

Remain Calm is a horror short by Jake Lewis of the Lewis Brothers, starring Pauly Shore, Nick Swardson, and Doug Jones. Yes, it does have some comedy overtones among the terrifying scenes that have commenters asking for more episodes starring the two store cashiers, or a full-length movie, or even a series following these characters. items.title: The Tingler
items.author: Miss Cellania
items.content:
The 1959 horror film The Tingler involves Vincent Price discovering a parasite that attaches to a person's spine. When they are afraid, the parasite grows stronger, and when they scream, it grows weaker. So it is to the tingler's advantage to scare the victim, and if you can't scream for some reason, you're a goner. But there's more than a monster in this movie- there's murder, too. 

Producer and director William Castle often used gimmicks for his films. For The Tingler, a method he called Percepto! was used. A buzzer device was installed in some theater seats that relayed a "tingle" at certain points int he movie. The audience was encouraged to scream if they felt it, because that would relieve the effects of the parasite. They also staged medical emergencies among some audiences. The Tingler wasn't all that well-received at the time, but has become a cult classic because of its camp qualities and Vincent Price's performance. (Thanks, WTM!)

items.title: Why Ghosts Wear White Sheets
items.author: Miss Cellania
items.content:
There was one time I actually went trick-or-treating as a ghost wearing a bed sheet with two eye holes. Just once. I learned that it's impossible to keep the eye holes in the right place when you're walking, or doing anything. I guess that's why Charlie Brown had multiple eye holes cut into his sheet. When my kid wanted to be a ghost, I insisted on using a white bathrobe with a (non-pointy)  hood and plenty of white face paint. She changed that to a black robe with white face paint and was much scarier. 

But why are ghosts depicted as being covered in a white sheet? The art that makes them look like that goes back further than the trick-or-treat costume. Even today, when very few kids want to be a ghost for Halloween, we hang up balloons with white fabric over them to decorate our porches, because that says "ghosts" to us. Dr. Emily Zarka of Monstrum explains why.

items.title: An Owl Uses Sound to Hunt Under the Snow
items.author: Miss Cellania
items.content:
If you're a rodent out in the forest, there's nothing more frightening than a hungry owl. They stare at you with those super predator eyes and glide in silently for the kill. Under a thick blanket of snow, however, they can't see you. 

The great grey owl will find you anyway. These birds have superpowers, and they can hear voles moving underneath the snow. They have excellent hearing, and their whole face is designed to enhance that ability. We need special effects to detect what the owl can hear. They also use physics to fine-tune their attack on a fast-moving vole they cannot see. The owl's survival depends on it. 

This nature sequence is from the CBC show The Nature of Things, from a series called Secret World of Sound. If you're interested, you can see how they got this amazing footage in a behind the scenes video explaining the acoustic camera. (via kottke)

items.title: The History of Domino's
items.author: Miss Cellania
items.content:
The original title of this video is How Domino's Became #1 With Bad Pizza, but I'm not using that because many folks like Domino's pizza. I haven't eaten one in I don't know how long and besides, pizza is like sex. Anyway, Domino's is the number one pizza chain, and often it's the only name people can remember. Most of that is the work of Tom Monaghan, who founded Domino's in 1960 with his younger brother Jim. Success came from hard work, streamlining the restaurant's menu, delivery, and inventing of the pizza box. Name recognition came, too. 

In the last 60 years, there have been many Domino's Pizza news stories that you will recall once you hear them again. Not all were detrimental to the company. but they all add up to a pizza place that everyone knows, even if they don't particularly care for the pizza.

items.title: Paid Vacation
items.author: Miss Cellania
items.content:
You will not be surprised that that United States has no mandatory paid days off for workers. But you might be surprised that we are the ONLY nation with over a million people that does not mandate any paid days off for workers. Gig work doesn't have any paid time off at all. In radio, most stations I worked for gave you a week's vacation if you lasted a whole year. However, they always made you feel bad for taking it. And you had to work extra hours for anyone else who took one, so we paid for it during the year and management wasn't out any cash. The rest of the world doesn't expect everybody to work all the time forever.

The ROV (remotely operated vehicle) Hercules was down 323 meters (1059 feet) in the Papahānaumokuākea National Marine Sanctuary west of Hawaii, looking around for researchers aboard the EV Nautilus. A small octopus was just doing octopus things when the ROV's measurement lights became clear on the ocean floor. What did the octopus do? It chased the lights, just like a cat would chase a laser toy, much to the delight of the scientists watching it. 

That's only the first two minutes of this video. There are other clips of small octopi looking for hidey holes and changing their colors. And as usual, the most delightful part of Nautilus' videos are the remarks from the researchers, who do this all the time and still find wonder in watching deep sea creatures in a their natural habitat. (via Metafilter)

items.title: Mr. Sardonicus
items.author: Miss Cellania
items.content:
In the 1961 Willian Castle gothic horror film Mr. Sardonicus, physician Sir Robert Cargrave is summoned by his ex-girlfriend Maude to a spooky eastern European castle to treat her new husband, Baron Sardonicus. The Baron suffers from a face paralyzed into an evil grin that interferes with eating and speaking -a result of his grave robbing incident. He rules his roost with cruelty, and Dr. Cargrave is drawn into his plans to cure his malady with experimental procedures because he's afraid of what may happen to Maude. (Thanks, WTM!)

items.title: Stutterer
items.author: Miss Cellania
items.content:
Greenwood (played by Matthew Needham) is a lonely typographer who suffers from a serious stutter, and it makes his life hard. He's found ways around it to some extent, but everyday tasks are a constant reminder of his disability, like trying to get through to a customer service representative on the phone. His thoughts, however, are fluid and even poetic. The bright spot is that he's built a long distance text relationship with a woman named Ellie. Greenwood's anxiety blows up to eleven when she has an opportunity to travel to London and meet him in person. 

The short film Stutterer highlights the inner struggles of those who suffer from a condition most of us don't understand. The film won an Oscar in 2016 for Best Live Action Short Film, plus a slew of other awards, and is only now available for all of us to see. I highly recommend it. (via kottke)
